name: Akkadian Empire
summary: Often called the first empire, founded by Sargon of Akkad. It united the Sumerian city-states under one king and made Akkadian the common language.

location.value: Mesopotamia, ruled from the city of Akkad, whose location has never been found.

terrain.value: The Tigris and Euphrates river plains, with campaigns into Syria, Anatolia and Iran.
terrain.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

climate.value: Severe drought linked to the 4.2-kiloyear climate event contributed to the collapse.

resources.value: Grain from irrigated fields; metals, timber and stone had to be brought from abroad.
resources.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

disasters.value: A major drought around 2200 BCE (the “4.2-kiloyear event”) may have helped bring the empire down.

population.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

urbanisation.value: Sumerian cities (Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Nippur) plus Akkad itself.
urbanisation.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

disease.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

migration.value: Pressure from Gutians and Amorites on the empire’s edges.

economicBase.value: Irrigation agriculture and temple and palace estates.
economicBase.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

tradeRoutes.value: Trade along the Gulf with Magan (Oman) and Meluhha (the Indus Valley).
tradeRoutes.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

moneyAndTax.value: No coinage. Grain and silver were used to measure value, with standardised measures (the gur of about 300 litres).
moneyAndTax.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

inequality.value: Kings, governors and temple elites at the top; dependent labourers at the bottom.
inequality.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

governmentType.value: Monarchy with provinces run by governors (ensi).

keyRulers.value: Sargon (c. 2334–2279 BCE), Rimush, Manishtushu, Naram-Sin (c. 2254–2218 BCE), Shar-Kali-Sharri.

succession.value: Hereditary, from father to son, often with revolts at each change of ruler.
succession.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

institutions.value: Royal governors over the city-states and standardised weights and measures.
institutions.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

stability.value: Repeated revolts, including the Great Revolt against Naram-Sin.

eliteConflict.value: Sumerian city elites resented Akkadian rule; Rimush and Manishtushu may both have been murdered.
eliteConflict.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

armyAndTech.value: A standing army, said to include 5,400 men who ate daily before Sargon.
armyAndTech.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

majorWars.value: Conquest of the Sumerian cities and campaigns in Elam, Syria and Anatolia.

territoryChange.value: Perhaps about 800,000 km² around 2250 BCE, from the Persian Gulf to Syria.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Elam, the Gutians and the Amorites.

inventions.value: A standardised system of measures and the first large-scale use of royal propaganda in art.
inventions.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

scienceEducation.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

openness.value: Combined Sumerian and Akkadian culture; Akkadian became the main language of the region.
openness.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

religion.value: Mesopotamian religion. Naram-Sin declared himself a living god.

languageWriting.value: Akkadian became the lingua franca, written in cuneiform; Sumerian was kept for religion.

artsArchitecture.value: The Victory Stele of Naram-Sin and the bronze “Mask of Sargon”.

socialStructure.value: King, governors, priests, scribes, farmers and slaves.
socialStructure.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

sharedIdentity.value: The title “King of the Four Quarters” (of the world).

neighbours.value: Elam, the Gutians, Amorites, Ebla, and trade partners Magan and Meluhha.

ideasReligions.value: Its model of empire inspired later Mesopotamian kings for 2,000 years.
ideasReligions.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

colonisation.value: Placed governors and garrisons in conquered cities.
colonisation.source: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (2016)

riseSignals.value: Sargon’s conquest of the Sumerian city-states.

peakPeriod.value: Under Naram-Sin, with the empire at its largest.

declineSignals.value: Revolts, invasions by the Gutians, and severe drought.

outcome.value: Collapse around 2154 BCE, followed by the Gutian period and then the Third Dynasty of Ur.

sources.value: Royal inscriptions, Sumerian King List, later legends. Checked against Wikipedia (“Akkadian Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Low to medium. Dates differ between chronologies (Sargon’s accession is placed at 2334, 2316 or 2285 BCE).

knownFor.label: Sargon of Akkad
knownFor.note: Founder of what is often called the first empire.

knownFor.label: Enheduanna
knownFor.note: Sargon’s daughter, a priestess and poet often called the first known named author.

knownFor.label: Victory Stele of Naram-Sin
knownFor.note: A carved stone showing the king climbing a mountain over his enemies.

knownFor.label: Akkadian as a lingua franca
knownFor.note: Akkadian, written in cuneiform, became the common language of the Near East.
